title: Single-spike superradiant free-electron lasers
summary: Free-electron lasers (FELs) deliver high-brilliance radiation from the infrared to X-rays, enabling atomic-scale studies on femtosecond-to-attosecond timescales. Yet conventional facilities rely on large, costly radio-frequency accelerators. Laser wakefield accelerators (LWFAs), combining high accelerating gradients with ultra-high peak currents, offer a compact alternative and open up new prospects for advanced FEL operation. Here, we demonstrate a tabletop superradiant FEL driven by single-spike, pre-bunched electron beams from a LWFA. By manipulating the energy chirp during acceleration and compressing the bunch to sub-wavelength duration, we obtain coherent radiation extending into the vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) regime within a remarkably compact 3-metre beamline--from gas target to radiator. Under optimized conditions, the measured photon yield reaches 2.8x10^10 per pulse after transmission through a 500-um slit, with a reproducibility of approximately 70%. This approach uniquely exploits the energy chirp and high-current characteristics inherent to LWFA beams without recourse to exponential gain, substantially minimizing device length while obviating the need for external synchronization and offering enhanced tolerance to jitter--thereby establishing a practical route toward efficient, compact FELs suitable for applications in academic, industrial, and clinical settings.

AI.tldr: A tabletop superradiant free-electron laser driven by single-spike, pre-bunched laser-wakefield-accelerated electron beams generates coherent vacuum-ultraviolet radiation in a 3-metre beamline with high photon yield and about 70% reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Conventional free-electron lasers require large, costly radio-frequency accelerators; laser wakefield accelerators offer compact high-gradient acceleration and ultra-high peak currents, motivating compact advanced FEL schemes.
AI.method: The authors use single-spike, pre-bunched electron beams from a laser wakefield accelerator, manipulate the energy chirp during acceleration, and compress the bunch to sub-wavelength duration to drive a superradiant FEL without exponential gain in a 3-metre beamline from gas target to radiator.
AI.result: Coherent radiation extending into the vacuum ultraviolet was obtained; under optimized conditions, the measured photon yield reached 2.8x10^10 per pulse after transmission through a 500-um slit, with approximately 70% reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: The approach exploits LWFA energy chirp and high current while minimizing device length, avoiding external synchronization, and improving tolerance to jitter, providing a practical route toward efficient compact FELs for academic, industrial, and clinical applications.

title: Evidence for MeV Radiation from a Large-Amplitude Crystalline Undulator
summary: We report evidence for MeV radiation from a large-amplitude crystalline undulator in which 35 GeV/c positrons channel along periodically bent Si(110) planes. Si$_3$N$_4$ stressors produce ten periods with $λ_u = 334~μ$m and midplane amplitude $A_u \simeq 1.85$ nm (XRD-validated modeling). Under planar alignment, the energy-loss spectrum shows an excess over the misaligned case peaking at $6.8 \pm 0.3$ MeV ($4.05σ$), in agreement with simulations and the 7.2 MeV analytical estimate. Simulations for 20 GeV FCC-ee injector positrons predict a peak brilliance of $1.8\times10^{21}$ photons/(s mm$^2$ mrad$^2$ 0.1% BW).

title: An Analytical Model for Fast Design Optimization and Performance Studies of nuSTORM
summary: The concept of generating neutrino beams from stored muons (nuSTORM) has been explored for several decades. A few nuSTORM facilities have been designed for GeV muons, and a design of a sub-GeV nuSTORM, proposed for the European Spallation Source, is now underway. At low energy, the much larger beam divergence can significantly reduce the neutrino flux reaching the detector. Therefore, optimization of facility parameters is essential to avoid additional flux losses. This optimization, however, is not trivial due to the interdependency of the parameters. In this paper, we derive an analytical expression for the absolute neutrino flux incident on the detector front face and show how it can guide the optimization of a nuSTORM facility. The analytical expression is furthermore validated with published data and Monte Carlo simulations from five separate cases. In addition, we show how it can be extended to also predict the neutrino energy distribution at the detector, thus offering a convenient method to estimate the facility performance without time-consuming Monte Carlo simulations of particle transport and decay.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an analytical model for the absolute neutrino flux at the detector of a nuSTORM facility and uses it to support fast design optimization and performance estimation, including extension to neutrino energy distributions, reducing reliance on detailed Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.motivation: At low muon energies, large beam divergence can substantially reduce the neutrino flux reaching the detector, so facility parameters must be optimized to avoid additional flux losses. Such optimization is nontrivial because the parameters are interdependent.
AI.method: The authors derive an analytical expression for the absolute neutrino flux incident on the detector front face and show how it can guide nuSTORM facility optimization. They validate the expression against published data and Monte Carlo simulations from five separate cases, and extend it to predict the neutrino energy distribution at the detector.
AI.result: The analytical expression is validated with published data and Monte Carlo simulations from five separate cases. It can also be extended to predict the detector neutrino energy distribution, enabling facility performance estimates without time-consuming Monte Carlo simulations of particle transport and decay.
AI.conclusion: The proposed analytical model provides a convenient and validated means for fast design optimization and performance studies of nuSTORM facilities, particularly by guiding parameter optimization and avoiding some computationally expensive Monte Carlo simulations.

title: Spectroscopy of ultracold molecules in the mid-infrared
summary: Unlike the microwave and optical domains, frequency metrology in the mid-infrared has not yet benefited from the long coherence times and exquisite control provided by ultracold particles. We use a quantum cascade laser operating at 17.5 THz to drive ro-vibrational transitions in ultracold calcium monofluoride molecules. The laser linewidth is narrowed to 15 kHz by locking it to a custom mid-infrared ring cavity, which is in turn locked to an ultrastable laser. We study the spectrum for molecules confined in red-detuned and blue-detuned magneto-optical traps, and in an optical dipole trap. In the dipole trap, the spectroscopic linewidth is close to that of the laser. We consider the stability and accuracy that can be reached using these methods in the context of a broader programme for improving frequency metrology in the mid-infrared.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates mid-infrared ro-vibrational spectroscopy of ultracold calcium monofluoride molecules using a narrow-linewidth quantum cascade laser locked to a mid-infrared ring cavity and an ultrastable laser, achieving a 15 kHz laser linewidth and near-laser-limited spectroscopic linewidth in an optical dipole trap.
AI.motivation: Mid-infrared frequency metrology has not yet exploited the long coherence times and precise control available with ultracold particles, unlike the microwave and optical domains. The authors aim to extend such capabilities to mid-infrared spectroscopy and assess paths toward improved frequency metrology.
AI.method: A quantum cascade laser operating at 17.5 THz is frequency-narrowed to 15 kHz by locking it to a custom mid-infrared ring cavity, which is itself locked to an ultrastable laser. The laser drives ro-vibrational transitions of ultracold calcium monofluoride molecules confined in red-detuned and blue-detuned magneto-optical traps and in an optical dipole trap.
AI.result: The laser linewidth is reduced to 15 kHz. Spectra are obtained for molecules in both magneto-optical trap configurations and in the optical dipole trap. In the dipole trap, the spectroscopic linewidth is close to the laser linewidth. The abstract does not provide detailed transition frequencies, uncertainties, or specific stability and accuracy values.
AI.conclusion: The methods enable mid-infrared spectroscopy of ultracold molecules with linewidth approaching the narrowed laser linewidth in an optical dipole trap. title: Laser cooling of $\mathrm{Th}^{-}$: Revised bound-state structure and a more efficient cooling scheme
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 1 table (main text); Supplemental Material included
summary: The thorium anion ($\mathrm{Th}^{-}$) has been proposed as a candidate for laser cooling of negative ions. However, previous theoretical and experimental results exhibit significant discrepancies in both the excitation energies and lifetimes. Here we revisit the bound-state structure and transition properties of $\mathrm{Th}^{-}$ using two independent ab initio approaches. The two calculations agree well and improve agreement with measured excitation energies and lifetimes. Based on the present level structure, we reassign several observed levels and show that the previously proposed $^4F^e_{3/2}\leftrightarrow{}^2S^o_{1/2}$ cooling transition is not closed and requires two repumping lasers. We therefore propose an alternative cooling scheme based on the $^4F^e_{3/2}\leftrightarrow{}^4F^o_{3/2}$ transition, which requires only one repumping laser and has a transition rate approximately five times larger ($A\approx1.1\times10^5$ s$^{-1}$), the fastest reported bound--bound E1 transition in atomic anions to date.

AI.method: The authors perform two independent ab initio calculations of the bound-state structure and transition properties of Th−, compare them with measured excitation energies and lifetimes, reassign several observed levels, and evaluate alternative laser-cooling transitions. The specific ab initio methods are not named in the abstract.

title: Buffer-Gas-Assisted Fluorescence Spectroscopy of Molecular Ions
summary: Sustained fluorescence detection of generic molecules has been challenging due to the lack of cycling transitions and limited photon budgets. We demonstrate a nondestructive method for continuous fluorescence of strongly rovibronically open molecular ions, $^{232}$ThF$^+$. Effective quasi-cycling transitions are established by room-temperature buffer-gas collisions, which replenish the population back to the laser-addressed states. In situ images and rotationally resolved spectra are obtained without optical repumping or auxiliary atomic readout ions. Combined with low-background spectroscopic detection, this approach achieves a signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 6 in a 1 s exposure on the P(1) line of $^{232}$ThF$^+$, despite a thermal population of only approximately 0.17% in the addressed state at room temperature. The ability to repeatedly interrogate trapped ions is particularly promising for scarce molecular samples, broadband spectroscopic searches, and in situ monitoring of molecular reactions.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates continuous, nondestructive fluorescence spectroscopy of strongly rovibronically open 232ThF+ molecular ions using room-temperature buffer-gas collisions to create effective quasi-cycling transitions, achieving rotationally resolved spectra and in situ imaging without optical repumping or auxiliary atomic readout ions.
AI.motivation: Sustained fluorescence detection of generic molecules is challenging because of the lack of cycling transitions and limited photon budgets. The work aims to enable repeated interrogation of trapped molecular ions, which is promising for scarce molecular samples, broadband spectroscopic searches, and in situ monitoring of molecular reactions.
AI.method: Room-temperature buffer-gas collisions are used to replenish population back to laser-addressed states, establishing effective quasi-cycling transitions in strongly rovibronically open 232ThF+. In situ images and rotationally resolved spectra are obtained without optical repumping or auxiliary atomic readout ions, combined with low-background spectroscopic detection.

AI.conclusion: Buffer-gas-assisted fluorescence spectroscopy enables continuous and repeated interrogation of trapped molecular ions without optical repumping or auxiliary atomic readout ions, with particular promise for scarce molecular samples, broadband spectroscopic searches, and in situ monitoring of molecular reactions.

title: Quantum-logic detection of rotationally inelastic collisions of single molecules
summary: Collisions between molecules govern chemical reactions and energy transfer across a range of different environments from interstellar space to the Earth's atmosphere. Despite their fundamental importance, molecular collisions have traditionally been studied through ensemble-averaged experiments which obscure the dynamics of individual scattering events on the quantum level. Probing single molecular collisions with quantum-state resolution has thus far remained a major experimental challenge. Here, we demonstrate a method for detecting individual rotationally inelastic collisions of single molecular ions with neutral atoms using quantum-logic techniques. We prepare individual trapped N$_2^+$ ions in their rotational ground state, subject them to a beam of helium atoms and detect isolated collision events through their effects on the motion of the trapped ions. Quantum-logic-spectroscopic measurements reveal changes of the molecular state upon collision enabling the determination of the probability of rotationally inelastic scattering. The experiments are analysed by comparison with quantum and classical scattering calculations yielding detailed insights into the underlying collision dynamics. By combining single-collision detection with non-destructive readout of the molecular quantum state, our approach establishes a new experimental framework for investigating molecular scattering beyond conventional ensemble measurements. It opens a route towards investigating state-to-state scattering in individual molecules and exploring molecular interactions at the level of single quantum-state resolved events.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates quantum-logic detection of individual rotationally inelastic collisions between single trapped N2+ molecular ions and neutral helium atoms, resolving collision-induced changes in the molecular quantum state and comparing observations with quantum and classical scattering calculations.
AI.motivation: Molecular collisions are fundamental to chemical reactions and energy transfer, but conventional ensemble-averaged experiments obscure individual quantum-level scattering events; probing single molecular collisions with quantum-state resolution has remained a major experimental challenge.
AI.method: Single N2+ ions are trapped and prepared in their rotational ground state, exposed to a helium-atom beam, and monitored for isolated collision events through their effects on trapped-ion motion. Quantum-logic spectroscopy provides non-destructive readout of the molecular state, enabling determination of the rotationally inelastic scattering probability; results are analyzed using quantum and classical scattering calculations.
AI.result: The experiments detect individual rotationally inelastic collisions, reveal collision-induced changes in the molecular state, determine the probability of rotationally inelastic scattering, and provide detailed insights into the underlying collision dynamics through comparison with quantum and classical calculations.
AI.conclusion: Combining single-collision detection with non-destructive quantum-state readout establishes a new experimental framework for molecular scattering beyond ensemble measurements and opens a route toward state-to-state scattering studies of individual molecules at the level of single quantum-state-resolved events.

title: Optical trapping of neutral atoms via magnetic-dipole transitions
summary: Optical trapping of neutral atoms is almost universally described as an electric-dipole (E1) effect. We show that the magnetic field of light, acting on a magnetic-dipole (M1) transition, can induce an ac Zeeman shift significantly larger than the ac Stark shift, thereby enabling magnetic trapping. We construct the M1 polarizability tensor and identify a critical detuning $δ_c$, independent of optical power, below which the magnetic interaction dominates. We analyze suitable trapping parameters and possible loss mechanisms, particularly for the intraconfigurational transitions $^3H_6\rightarrow{}^3H_5$ of erbium at $1437.13$~nm and $^5I_8\rightarrow{}^5I_7$ of dysprosium at $2418.84$~nm. We propose two trapping configurations: a hybrid magnetic/electric optical tweezer and an optical lattice with separated magnetic and electric antinodes, producing state-dependent purely magnetic and purely electric trapping wells. Our results present optical magnetic fields as a suitable resource to expand the toolbox for atomic manipulation.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the magnetic field of light acting on a magnetic-dipole transition can produce an ac Zeeman shift larger than the ac Stark shift, enabling magnetic optical trapping of neutral atoms; it develops the M1 polarizability tensor, identifies a power-independent critical detuning, analyzes erbium and dysprosium transitions and loss mechanisms, and proposes hybrid tweezer and optical-lattice trapping schemes.
AI.motivation: Optical trapping of neutral atoms is generally treated as an electric-dipole effect. The authors aim to establish the optical magnetic field, via magnetic-dipole transitions, as an additional and potentially dominant mechanism for atomic manipulation.
AI.method: The authors construct the magnetic-dipole (M1) polarizability tensor and derive a critical detuning below which magnetic interaction dominates the electric ac Stark shift. They analyze trapping parameters and loss mechanisms for the erbium 3H6 to 3H5 transition at 1437.13 nm and the dysprosium 5I8 to 5I7 transition at 2418.84 nm, and propose a hybrid magnetic/electric optical tweezer and an optical lattice with separated magnetic and electric antinodes.
AI.result: The magnetic field of light can induce an ac Zeeman shift significantly larger than the ac Stark shift for an M1 transition. A critical detuning independent of optical power separates magnetic- and electric-dominated regimes. The proposed configurations can produce state-dependent purely magnetic and purely electric trapping wells. Experimental demonstration details are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Optical magnetic fields can serve as a suitable resource for expanding the toolbox of neutral-atom manipulation, including magnetic trapping and state-dependent trapping geometries.

title: Bayesian determination of structural ensembles from single-particle X-ray scattering images
summary: Single-particle X-ray scattering with free electron lasers records snapshots of individual molecules with femtosecond time resolution and is therefore ideally suited to study structural heterogeneity or molecular motions. Current approaches to determine structural ensembles rely on prior classification of the scattering images, which is error-prone and becomes infeasible for single macromolecules, whose images contain too few coherently scattered photons. Here, we present a Bayesian approach that samples weighted ensembles of electron densities directly from the posterior probability distribution given all scattering images, thereby avoiding classification altogether. We demonstrate our approach in the low signal-to-noise high heterogeneity regime using synthetic scattering data of a small and flexible protein, as well as on published experimental scattering images for the coliphage PR772 virus.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian approach infers weighted ensembles of electron densities directly from single-particle X-ray scattering images, avoiding prior image classification, and is demonstrated on synthetic low-signal heterogeneous data and experimental PR772 virus images.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for determining structural ensembles from free-electron-laser single-particle X-ray scattering rely on prior classification of scattering images, which is error-prone and infeasible for single macromolecules whose images contain too few coherently scattered photons.
AI.method: The paper samples weighted ensembles of electron densities directly from the posterior probability distribution conditioned on all scattering images, bypassing classification. It demonstrates the approach using synthetic scattering data for a small flexible protein in a low signal-to-noise, high-heterogeneity regime and published experimental scattering images of coliphage PR772 virus.
AI.result: The Bayesian method is demonstrated on synthetic low-signal, high-heterogeneity scattering data and on published experimental PR772 virus images. The abstract does not provide quantitative performance metrics.
AI.conclusion: Direct Bayesian posterior sampling of structural ensembles can avoid error-prone classification and supports studies of structural heterogeneity or molecular motions from single-particle X-ray scattering; the abstract does not detail broader validation or quantitative performance.

title: Rotor-driven piecewise cross polarization of wide quadrupolar lines: bath-contact pumping of vector and tensor order in dynamically polarized solids
summary: In a dynamically polarized solid with a common nuclear spin temperature, spin-1 $^{14}$N in ammonia sits at $P_N\simeq0.14$ when the protons are at $0.90$, and a deuteron in a proton-rich matrix at $P_D\simeq0.29$. Hartmann--Hahn cross polarization (CP) from the protons could raise either toward $P_H$, but the first-order quadrupole interaction spreads the $^{14}$N line over $5$~MHz at $5$~T, far beyond any single contact bandwidth. We develop the theory of CP into one transition of a quadrupolar spin-1, with slow sample rotation carrying each crystallite through a fixed-frequency contact window. A bath contact is an idempotent map on the populations of the contacted transition, so repeated or continuous contacts accumulate rather than cancel, and the hit-once and parity constraints that force stepped rotation for pulsed inversions do not arise. In the small-reservoir limit the population ratio across the contacted transition becomes $(1+P_H)/(1-P_H)$, giving $\Pzz=+0.88$ in one contact and $\Pzz\to-1.8$ in two from $P_H=0.9$, beyond the unitary bound $[-0.85,+0.65]$. Under continuous rotation, a window at the Pake horn reaches every bond for an axis perpendicular to the field, while a window in the clean pedestal region, needed for a definite sign of tensor order, reaches a fraction $\sin2θ_c=0.943$ at the magic angle $54.74\degree$. Steady-state order is set by the contact rate against rotation-driven cross-branch relaxation, negligible for $^{14}$N. In the cubic limit one contact places the spin-1 at the proton temperature ($\Pzz=+0.85$), but only a resolved quadrupole splitting permits negative tensor order. The limiting resource is the proton spin lock, which must far exceed the $\simeq28$~kHz local field for a contact short compared with $T_{1ρ}$, unmeasured at $1$~K. Protocols are given for $^{14}$N in NH$_3$ and deuterons in NH$_2$D.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theory for Hartmann–Hahn cross polarization into a single transition of quadrupolar spin-1 nuclei in dynamically polarized solids, using slow sample rotation to carry crystallites through a fixed-frequency contact window. It predicts accumulation of vector and tensor order beyond the unitary bound and provides protocols for 14N in NH3 and deuterons in NH2D, without reporting experimental validation.
AI.motivation: In dynamically polarized solids, protons can be highly polarized while 14N and deuterons remain at lower polarization. Cross polarization could raise either toward the proton polarization, but first-order quadrupole broadening spreads the 14N line over 5 MHz at 5 T, far beyond any single contact bandwidth, motivating piecewise, rotation-driven contacts.
AI.method: The authors develop a theory of cross polarization into one transition of a quadrupolar spin-1, with slow sample rotation carrying each crystallite through a fixed-frequency contact window. A bath contact is modeled as an idempotent map on the contacted-transition populations, so repeated or continuous contacts accumulate rather than cancel. The analysis includes the small-reservoir limit, continuous-rotation coverage for a Pake-horn window and a clean pedestal window at the magic angle, steady-state order set by contact rate versus rotation-driven cross-branch relaxation, and the cubic limit.
AI.result: In the small-reservoir limit, the population ratio across the contacted transition becomes (1+P_H)/(1-P_H), giving Pzz=+0.88 in one contact and Pzz→-1.8 in two from P_H=0.9, beyond the unitary bound [-0.85,+0.65]. Under continuous rotation, a Pake-horn window reaches every bond for an axis perpendicular to the field, while a pedestal window reaches a fraction sin2θc=0.943 at the magic angle 54.74°. In the cubic limit, one contact gives Pzz=+0.85, but negative tensor order requires a resolved quadrupole splitting. The limiting resource is the proton spin lock, which must far exceed the ~28 kHz local field for a contact short compared with T1ρ, unmeasured at 1 K.
AI.conclusion: Rotation-driven cross polarization can pump vector and tensor order piecewise without the hit-once and parity constraints that force stepped rotation for pulsed inversions. Protocols are proposed for 14N in NH3 and deuterons in NH2D. The work is theoretical; no experimental validation or 1 K T1ρ measurement is provided.

title: Multi-domain AAA-least squares methods and applications
comment: Submitted to SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics (Nov 2026)
summary: A multi-domain AAA-least squares (nAAALS) method is developed for computing rational approximations of harmonic functions defined in the interior and exterior of multiply-connected domains. Three classes of problems are considered: i) multi-domain problems where an unbounded exterior is punctured by multiple singly-connected domains; ii) nested domain problems where one domain contains multiple punctured domains; and iii) quasi-steady time-stepping problems where the nAAALS algorithm is coupled with standard Runge-Kutta schemes to compute the coupled evolution of the multiple domain boundaries. The nAAALS method extends the original AAALS algorithm in two key ways. First, a function $\tilde{S}$ satisfying $\tilde{S}(z)=\overline{z}$ on each domain boundary is approximated using the AAA algorithm, producing simple poles distributed according to both the individual boundary geometries and the global multi-domain configuration. Second, the least-squares framework is modified to accommodate the coupled matching conditions across each domain boundary. The method is applied to problems in vortex dynamics to demonstrate its capability, focusing specifically on vortex patches as a working example: finite-area regions of incompressible, inviscid fluid in rotational flow. The nAAALS algorithm is used to (a) reproduce known vortex patch equilibria, and (b) compute the evolution of new and existing non-equilibrium configurations. The results are shown to be accurate at low computational cost, running in seconds on a standard laptop. Crucially, the nAAALS method is suitable for addressing a broader class of steady and quasi-steady multi-domain problems across disciplines, such as those arising in applied mathematics, mathematical biology, and fluid dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a multi-domain AAA-least squares (nAAALS) method for rational approximation of harmonic functions in interior and exterior multiply-connected domains, including nested, punctured, and quasi-steady time-stepping configurations. It extends AAALS by using AAA to approximate a boundary-conjugate function and by modifying least squares for coupled matching conditions, then demonstrates the method on vortex-patch equilibria and evolution.
AI.motivation: The work is motivated by the need to compute rational approximations of harmonic functions in complex multi-domain settings, including unbounded exteriors punctured by multiple domains, nested domains, and quasi-steady coupled boundary evolution. The authors also aim to provide a method applicable to a broader class of steady and quasi-steady multi-domain problems across disciplines.

For quasi-steady problems, nAAALS is coupled with standard Runge-Kutta schemes. The method is demonstrated on vortex patches, i.e., finite-area regions of incompressible, inviscid rotational flow.

The results are reported as accurate at low computational cost, running in seconds on a standard laptop. No quantitative error values are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The nAAALS method is suitable for a broader class of steady and quasi-steady multi-domain problems across disciplines, including applied mathematics, mathematical biology, and fluid dynamics.

title: Dual-species atom interferometry for axion dark matter
summary: Atom interferometers are sensitive to oscillations of the masses and transition frequencies of atoms, which can be induced by axion dark matter. The main limitation is the sensitivity to gravity gradient noise (GGN). We propose a dual-species atom interferometry sequence that provides a suppression of GGN by up to three orders of magnitude and a sensitivity enhancement via the mass difference of the two atoms. We show that, under realistic experimental assumptions, a 10m-baseline dual-species atom interferometer is more sensitive to the axion gluon coupling than a 100m single-species gradiometer. Including a comprehensive noise analysis, we demonstrate that the Very Long Baseline Atom Interferometer (VLBAI) in Hannover with a baseline of 10m can probe the axion decay constant at levels almost competitive with leading laboratory constraints. The proposed 100m-baseline Atom Interferometer CERN Experiment (AICE) can extend this sensitivity by up to two orders of magnitude, surpassing laboratory constraints for axion masses of $10^{-19}\;\text{eV}/c^2 \lesssim m_a \lesssim 3\times10^{-15}\;\text{eV}/c^2$.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes dual-species atom interferometry to suppress gravity-gradient noise and enhance sensitivity to axion dark matter, showing that 10 m and 100 m baselines can probe axion-gluon and decay-constant parameter space competitively.
AI.motivation: Atom interferometers can detect axion-dark-matter-induced oscillations of atomic masses and transition frequencies, but their sensitivity is mainly limited by gravity gradient noise (GGN).
AI.method: The authors propose a dual-species atom interferometry sequence that suppresses GGN by up to three orders of magnitude and exploits the mass difference between two atomic species for sensitivity enhancement. They perform a comprehensive noise analysis for a 10 m VLBAI baseline and a proposed 100 m AICE baseline.
AI.result: Under realistic assumptions, a 10 m dual-species interferometer is more sensitive to the axion-gluon coupling than a 100 m single-species gradiometer. VLBAI can probe the axion decay constant at levels almost competitive with leading laboratory constraints, while AICE can extend sensitivity by up to two orders of magnitude and surpass laboratory constraints for axion masses from about 1e-19 eV/c^2 to 3e-15 eV/c^2.
AI.conclusion: Dual-species atom interferometry substantially mitigates GGN and improves axion dark matter sensitivity, making 10 m and 100 m baseline experiments competitive with or beyond leading laboratory constraints over a broad low-mass range.

title: Sphere-based test cases for open boundary simulations in electrostatics and magnetostatics
summary: This paper presents a library of sphere-based test cases for verifying the correctness of open boundary simulations in electrostatics and magnetostatics for computational physics and engineering applications. While the energy in the fields of a single sphere is computed for various source configurations, the energy, force and torque (when applicable) are also computed for a pair of spheres. An extension to electromagnetic momentum is also given for the single sphere, demonstrating its use as a benchmarking metric. Analytical expressions are provided for each test case, from which the validity of a simulation environment can be assessed. The finite element method is used as the example context, and four different open boundary methods are evaluated. Once verified, the simulation is used to visualize the Poynting vector field associated with an electric charge placed near a permanent magnet, a configuration for which no analytical expression is available. Simulation files are made available and all numerical experiments are reproducible with the ONELAB open source software.

AI.tldr: The paper provides analytical, sphere-based benchmark cases for verifying open-boundary electrostatics and magnetostatics simulations, demonstrates them with the finite element method and four open-boundary methods, and releases reproducible ONELAB simulation files.
AI.motivation: Open-boundary simulations in electrostatics and magnetostatics need reliable test cases to assess whether a simulation environment is correct for computational physics and engineering applications.
AI.method: A library of sphere-based test cases is constructed with analytical expressions. Single-sphere field energies are computed for various source configurations; for sphere pairs, energy, force, and torque (when applicable) are computed. Electromagnetic momentum is added as a single-sphere benchmarking metric. The finite element method is used as an example context, four open-boundary methods are evaluated, and a verified simulation visualizes the Poynting vector field for an electric charge near a permanent magnet, a configuration without an available analytical expression.
AI.result: Analytical expressions are provided for each test case, and four different open-boundary methods are evaluated in a finite element setting. title: Critical excited states in quantum metrology
summary: We investigate criticality-enhanced sensing near ground- and excited-state quantum phase transitions in a strongly coupled qubit-boson system. title: A Magnetic Neuroevolution Potential for Large Scale Spin-Lattice Simulations
summary: Accurately describing magnetic order, lattice vibrations, and their coupling at finite temperatures within a unified framework remains a major challenge in atomistic simulations of magnetic materials. In this work, we develop a magnetic neuroevolution potential that explicitly incorporates magnetic degrees of freedom, establishing a potential-energy description jointly determined by atomic structures and magnetic configurations and enabling unified predictions of atomic forces and magnetic energy gradients. Using CrN, Fe, and FeGe with collinear or noncollinear magnetic configurations as representative systems, we demonstrate that the model outperforms standard neuroevolution potentials without magnetic descriptors in predicting energies, atomic forces, and virials, while yielding equilibrium lattice constants consistent with experimental values. Phonon calculations for different magnetic states show that the model captures lattice vibrational responses to changes in magnetic order. Finite-temperature spin-lattice dynamics simulations further reveal the temperature dependence of magnetic excitation spectra, while calculations of the average atomic magnetic moment versus temperature demonstrate the influence of spin-lattice coupling on magnetic transition temperatures and system-size convergence. For Fe, explicitly including spin-lattice coupling brings the predicted magnetic transition temperature closer to experiment, whereas the difference in FeGe is smaller. Performance benchmarks demonstrate that the method enables coupled dynamics simulations of over two million atoms on a single consumer-grade GPU. By combining magnetic-configuration resolution with high computational efficiency, the framework provides an efficient tool for investigating finite-temperature dynamics and spin-lattice coupling in large-scale magnetic systems.

title: On the statistical reliability of chaotic simulations at reduced precision
summary: Reduced-precision arithmetic is increasingly used to accelerate scientific simulation, while AI workloads are driving its growing prominence in hardware design. Yet small arithmetic errors do not necessarily imply accurate statistics. Finite representation limits spatial resolution, while rounding can merge trajectories that should separate in chaotic systems, progressively concentrating probability on a shrinking collection of computer states. This redistribution can distort statistical averages well before periodicity becomes apparent; furthermore, disjoint computational basins can induce an initialisation bias, even when the intended equilibrium statistics are independent of the initial ensemble. We use functional graphs and their transfer operators to connect these pathologies to bounds on statistical bias, the duration of accurate averaging, and the effect of reducing precision. Exhaustive numerical experiments on four chaotic maps, with 1-24 significand bits and the 24-bit endpoint matching IEEE FP32, show how initially accurate ensembles drift towards incorrect statistics, with lower precision often bringing this deterioration forward. Stochastic rounding substantially extends some useful averaging windows but leaves others severely biased. Longer computed trajectories can therefore worsen inferred statistics, and a finite average can outperform the "infinite-time" computer average by orders of magnitude. This exposes a risk of statistically biased inference at reduced precision and provides a further motivation for collecting statistics from ensembles of shorter trajectories.

AI.tldr: Reduced-precision arithmetic can corrupt the statistical averages of chaotic simulations even when individual trajectories initially appear accurate. Using functional graphs and transfer operators, plus experiments on four chaotic maps across 1–24 significand bits, the paper shows that rounding-induced state merging and disjoint computational basins can bias statistics, shorten useful averaging windows, and make longer runs less reliable.
AI.motivation: Reduced-precision arithmetic is increasingly used to accelerate scientific simulation, and AI workloads are further promoting reduced precision in hardware design. title: Spatiotemporal learning improves quantification of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement
comment: 48 pages, 9 figures, 18 tables, including Supplementary Information
summary: Pore-space evolution and fluid displacement influence how rocks transmit and store fluids, affecting geological carbon storage, underground hydrogen storage and groundwater contaminant transport. A single time-resolved micro-CT experiment may produce tens to hundreds of three-dimensional images, and segmentation is required to quantify physical properties and run image-based simulations. Traditional methods such as thresholding perform poorly on noisy, low-contrast images and need manual adjustment per image; 3D deep learning networks segment each image without temporal information, so their errors vary between images and could be mistaken for physical change. Here we introduce a transformer-based 4D segmentation framework combining spatial and temporal information. It uses sequential images to resolve ambiguous phase assignments and separate physical change from segmentation error. The method is tested on images of mineral dissolution: it measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries more accurately than an equivalent 3D model that ignores temporal information. It also captures the increase in permeability verified against reference segmentations and flow simulations. The advantage transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining. On two other datasets of fluid displacement, it reduces spurious changes in predicted rock and porosity fluctuations and accurately identifies filling events. Spatiotemporal segmentation turns sequences of hundreds of three-dimensional images into more reliable quantitative measurements of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement without per-image parameter adjustment to support the analysis of time-resolved CT imaging.

AI.tldr: A transformer-based 4D segmentation framework uses spatial and temporal information from time-resolved micro-CT image sequences to improve quantification of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement.

AI.method: The paper introduces a transformer-based 4D segmentation framework that combines spatial and temporal information across sequential images to resolve ambiguous phase assignments and separate physical change from segmentation error. title: A Diffusive T-Matrix Unifying the Electric and Magnetic Polarizability Tensors in Conducting Layered Media
summary: Electromagnetic induction is used to detect and classify buried and submerged objects, such as unexploded ordnance in soil and on the seabed. A small object is commonly described by its magnetic polarizability tensor (MPT), which is independent of its position and of the sensor. The MPT assumes that the surrounding medium does not conduct. In seawater at extremely low frequency, or in clay at kilohertz frequencies, this assumption fails at depths comparable to the skin depth. The object then also diverts the current induced in the medium, a galvanic response that the MPT omits. We describe the object instead by its transition matrix (T-matrix), which keeps the independence from position and sensor and includes both responses. It is computed once per medium and frequency from a single finite element problem, for any shape and materials. Its inductive block reduces to the MPT when the medium conducts weakly, and its galvanic block reduces to the electric polarizability tensor in the static limit. We test the model against full finite element solutions for a conducting box, non-magnetic and permeable, in a layered sea and in clay over bedrock. Two orders beyond the dipole, it is accurate to within 1.4% over two decades of frequency and for sizes up to 0.7 of the depth, whereas the error of the MPT carried into the conducting medium reaches 91%. Blocks coupling the two responses, contained in neither tensor, contribute up to 13%.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a diffusive transition matrix (T-matrix) for small objects in conducting layered media, unifying magnetic and electric polarizability responses and capturing inductive, galvanic, and coupling effects that the magnetic polarizability tensor omits.
AI.motivation: The magnetic polarizability tensor (MPT) assumes a nonconducting surrounding medium and omits the galvanic response caused by an object diverting induced currents. This assumption fails in settings such as seawater at extremely low frequency or clay at kilohertz frequencies, motivating a position- and sensor-independent object description that includes both responses.
AI.method: The object is represented by a T-matrix computed once per medium and frequency from a single finite element problem for arbitrary shape and materials. Its inductive block reduces to the MPT under weak medium conduction, and its galvanic block reduces to the electric polarizability tensor in the static limit. The model is tested against full finite element solutions for conducting non-magnetic and permeable boxes in a layered sea and in clay over bedrock.
AI.result: Two orders beyond the dipole, the T-matrix model is accurate to within 1.4% over two decades of frequency and for object sizes up to 0.7 of the depth. The error of the MPT carried into the conducting medium reaches 91%, and coupling blocks contained in neither tensor contribute up to 13%.
AI.conclusion: The diffusive T-matrix provides an accurate, position- and sensor-independent description of conducting objects in conducting layered media, unifying magnetic and electric polarizability responses and capturing coupling effects absent from the MPT.

title: An Invariant Neural-Network Eddy-Viscosity Closure with Iterative Solver Coupling for Molten Salt Fast Reactor Thermal-Hydraulics
summary: System thermal-hydraulics codes such as the System Analysis Module (SAM) close turbulence on coarse meshes with algebraic zero-equation mixing-length models. These models cannot represent the non-equilibrium turbulence, flow separation, and large-scale recirculation of open-cavity advanced reactors. We develop an invariant neural-network eddy-viscosity closure for SAM and apply it to the Molten Salt Fast Reactor (MSFR). The closure predicts the turbulent kinetic energy and timescale of each element from the flow and geometry of its neighbors, without solving turbulence transport equations. The resulting non-negative eddy viscosity enters the implicit diffusive operator, which keeps the momentum equations well conditioned. We prove that the closure is exactly invariant to translation, Galilean boost, rotation, reflection, and neighbor ordering. A network trained on high-order Nek5000 fields sees a different feature distribution on the coarse SAM mesh. We remove this covariate shift by iteratively retraining the network on SAM flow states against fixed Nek5000 targets. For a held-out steady state, the coupled closure reproduces the single recirculation cell and eddy-viscosity plume of the Nek5000 reference. In a 120 s pump-coastdown transient, it halves the velocity error of the mixing-length model, from 37.6% to 17.7%, and matches the Nek5000 eddy viscosity with a time-averaged relative error of 12%. The remaining velocity error comes from the coarse mesh. The coupled transient takes about 0.2 core-hours, compared with about 330 core-hours for Nek5000. The results show that the closure can recover two-equation RANS turbulence behavior in a coarse-mesh system code at a small fraction of the CFD cost.

title: Distilling an atomistic foundation model is all you need for large-scale molecular dynamics of semiconductor interfaces
summary: State-of-the-art atomistic foundation models provide broadly transferable energy and force predictions, but their direct deployment in large-scale molecular dynamics remains computationally costly. Here we examine whether their knowledge can be distilled into compact potentials while retaining the physical responses of heterogeneous semiconductor interfaces. From 128 pretrained models spanning 22 model families, we select a fixed EquiformerV3 teacher and train atomic cluster expansion (ACE) and neuroevolution potential (NEP) students without target-specific teacher fine-tuning, with both simulation speed and accessible system size improved by several orders of magnitude relative to the teacher model. Matched training configurations and architectures enable direct comparisons with students trained on density-functional-theory (DFT) reference labels. For 79,920-atom BAs/GaN interfaces, direct distillation preserves termination-dependent thermal conductance and dominant spectral features, with conductance differing by at most 6.6% from DFT-trained counterparts. In 29,792-atom Cu/diamond specimens loaded at 500 K, tensile strength and loading work differ by 2.8% and 1.5%, respectively. Exploratory SiC/a-C/SiC simulations retain the principal thermal bottleneck and the direction of the annealing response. Furthermore, a four-model committee retrieves 42-56% of the highest-error teacher configurations with a 10% selection budget and improves high-error force fitting, but does not consistently improve downstream properties. These findings demonstrate that direct distillation can preserve key interfacial thermal and mechanical responses in compact interatomic potentials, opening a path towards large-scale, high-throughput simulations of heterogeneous interfaces.

title: Irreversible dynamics for ideal fluids on Riemannian manifolds: metriplectic energy-conserving alternatives to Navier-Stokes
comment: 32 pages, no figures, first version. All comments are welcome!
summary: For modelling dissipative phenomena such as friction, diffusion and viscosity, the Hamiltonian framework has a key limitation: once the Casimir invariants are fixed, Hamiltonian flows preserve phase-space volume, which rules out relaxation to equilibrium. Thus modelling dissipation requires modifying the Hamiltonian structure. Following the metriplectic (equivalently, GENERIC) approach, we add to the Hamiltonian vector field a dissipative term generated by a symmetric bracket, here constructed from a Riemannian metric. The resulting flow conserves the energy, and optionally further invariants, while driving a chosen generalised entropy monotonically, which makes the dynamics irreversible; when the entropy is bounded on energy level sets in the direction in which it is driven, it acts as a Lyapunov functional. We apply this construction to ideal fluids on compact Riemannian manifolds, choosing Casimirs of the Lie-Poisson bracket as entropies. In two dimensions, dissipating enstrophy yields the already-known energy-constrained Navier-Stokes equations, which include a nonlocal term restoring energy balance. In three dimensions, where enstrophy is no longer a Casimir, we derive new irreversible models. For incompressible and compressible fluids carrying an advected scalar, dissipating potential enstrophy or higher potential-vorticity moments gives a nonlinear, anisotropic diffusion that acts to align the gradients of the scalar and of the potential vorticity. For a purely incompressible fluid, taking helicity as the entropy gives a first-order, non-smoothing dissipative term whose stationary states are Beltrami fields.

AI.tldr: A metriplectic/GENERIC construction adds a Riemannian-metric-generated symmetric dissipative bracket to Hamiltonian ideal-fluid dynamics on compact Riemannian manifolds, conserving energy while monotonically driving Casimir-based entropies. It recovers energy-constrained Navier-Stokes in two dimensions and yields new irreversible three-dimensional fluid models, including anisotropic diffusion and a helicity-dissipating model with Beltrami stationary states.

AI.method: The authors add to the Hamiltonian vector field a dissipative term generated by a symmetric bracket constructed from a Riemannian metric. The flow conserves energy and optionally further invariants while monotonically driving a chosen generalized entropy, acting as a Lyapunov functional when the entropy is bounded on energy level sets in the driven direction. AI.conclusion: Metriplectic, metric-generated dissipation provides energy-conserving alternatives to Navier-Stokes for ideal fluids on Riemannian manifolds, unifying a known two-dimensional model with new three-dimensional irreversible models and identifying conditions under which the chosen entropy is a Lyapunov functional.

title: Asymmetric Frequency Conversion and Violation of Kirchhoff's Law of Thermal Radiation in Phased Floquet Metasurfaces
summary: We study a system of three closely spaced conducting sheets, whose thermal emission largely violates Kirchhoff's law through nonreciprocal frequency conversion enabled by Floquet phenomena. We leverage surface mode transitions controlled by temporal modulation of one of the metasurfaces, resulting in largely asymmetric frequency conversion. Our findings broaden the capabilities of Floquet metasurfaces for wave conversion and energy manipulation, paving the way towards magnet-free nonreciprocal photonic devices with opportunities for thermal management and efficient photonic refrigeration.

title: Plasma simulations with adaptive mesh and algorithm refinement
summary: Adaptive Mesh and Algorithm Refinement (AMAR) combines adaptive Cartesian meshes with automatic selection of kinetic or fluid solvers. It was introduced for rarefied gas dynamics and later extended to gas mixtures, particle and lattice-Boltzmann solvers, computational electromagnetics, and multi-phase flows. In weakly ionized plasmas, the species differ by orders of magnitude in mass, velocity, and time scale. This paper describes PAMAR, a plasma extension of AMAR in which electrons, ions, neutral species, and fields can have independent adaptive-mesh solvers, each with its own phase-space dimensionality, refinement criteria, and time step, coupled through a field solver in one executable built on the Basilisk framework. We present two demonstrations. A transient capacitively coupled plasma in argon is simulated with two-stream kinetic solvers for electrons and ions on independent adaptive quadtrees in $(x,v)$. The simulations resolve three electron groups and the time scales of electron and ion kinetics without statistical noise, at a cost between particle-in-cell simulations and fast kinetic models. A sphere at floating potential in a collisionless or weakly collisional plasma is computed with octree solvers in $(r,v,μ)$ for both species and compared with an exact method-of-characteristics solution. Per-species meshes resolve the cold ions at a tenth of the uniform-mesh cost. Both demonstrations also select the model cell by cell. In the capacitive discharge, a hybrid ion solver is kinetic in the sheaths and fluid in the bulk. Around the sphere, a hybrid electron solver confines the kinetic solver to the loss-cone layer and uses a Fokker-Planck model in position and total energy elsewhere. It conserves particles exactly across the interface and uses 1.6 to 5.3 times fewer cells. We discuss the next steps toward parallel, implicit simulations of higher-dimensional problems.

Demonstrations for a capacitively coupled argon discharge and a floating-potential sphere show resolved kinetic features, cell-by-cell hybrid model selection, particle conservation, and substantial mesh-cost reductions.

title: Rotationally Symmetric Lattice Boltzmann Pseudopotential Methods for Porous Media Applications
summary: Pseudopotential models are a well established approach for multiphase and multicomponent simulations using the lattice Boltzmann method. Although not the most accurate, they are often chosen for ease of implementation and adaptability. A drawback of the models are spurious currents at the interfaces and particularly at solid walls which introduce numerical artifacts. An improved lattice Boltzmann pseudopotential model is presented. The discrete fluid density gradients in the coupling force are computed with rotationally symmetric gradient operators formulated as a convolution. As a result, spurious currents are reduced in settings where solid walls are unaligned with the lattice directions. Additionally, variations of introducing fluid-solid interaction either equally through both fluids or through a single fluid only are compared. Presented model variants are compared using droplets on walls as a common benchmark, analytically solvable capillary rise experiments (Jurin's law), and porous media imbibition as a practical application. Rotationally symmetric operators outperform the classical lattice weights approach in all tests in terms of accuracy, while avoiding extending the lattice to compute higher order gradients. The choice of the fluid-solid interaction variant depends on the problem under consideration and the desired properties of the resulting model.

AI.tldr: An improved lattice Boltzmann pseudopotential model uses rotationally symmetric convolution-based density-gradient operators to reduce spurious currents, especially at solid walls unaligned with lattice directions, and is benchmarked on wall droplets, capillary rise, and porous-media imbibition.
AI.motivation: Pseudopotential lattice Boltzmann models are easy to implement and adaptable for multiphase/multicomponent simulation, but spurious currents at interfaces and solid walls introduce numerical artifacts, particularly when walls are not aligned with lattice directions.
AI.method: The discrete fluid density gradients in the coupling force are computed using rotationally symmetric gradient operators formulated as a convolution. Variants that introduce fluid-solid interaction equally through both fluids or through only one fluid are compared. Validation uses droplets on walls, analytically solvable capillary rise according to Jurin's law, and porous media imbibition.
AI.result: Rotationally symmetric operators outperform the classical lattice-weights approach in all tests in terms of accuracy while avoiding extension of the lattice to compute higher-order gradients. The preferred fluid-solid interaction variant depends on the problem and desired model properties.
AI.conclusion: The proposed rotationally symmetric pseudopotential formulation reduces spurious currents in settings with lattice-misaligned solid walls and provides accuracy gains without higher-order gradient lattices; fluid-solid interaction variants should be selected according to the application.

title: Pseudovortex-assisted generation of first-order vector modes
summary: A practical method of generating first-order vector modes like radially and azimuthally polarized modes is using the so-called vortex waveplates. Shining these plates with Gaussian beams produces parasitic higher-order modes besides the target vector beam. The reason is that there is a mismatch between the incident Gaussian mode and the doughnut-shaped profile required for the vector beam. This imposes a limit on the fidelity of the generated mode with respect to the target vector beam. In this work we demonstrate theoretically and experimentally that this limit can be overcome if the input Gaussian beam is replaced with a pseudovortex beam, which is a doughnut-shaped mode without topological charge. We use a spatial light modulator to generate this input mode and a geometric-phase-compensated triangular cavity for mode analysis. We demonstrate vector mode fidelity as high as $0.921 \pm 0.013$, which is considerably better than $0.815 \pm 0.003$ obtained with Gaussian input. We also investigate the fidelity as a function of the input beam waist, leading to a theoretical upper bound for the fidelity of $8π/27 \approx 0.931$, in close agreement with the experimental results. This approach presents a reliable method of generating high-fidelity vector modes.

AI.tldr: Replacing Gaussian input with a doughnut-shaped pseudovortex beam in vortex-waveplate generation reduces parasitic higher-order modes and raises first-order vector-mode fidelity from 0.815 to 0.921, with theory predicting an upper bound near 0.931.
AI.motivation: Vortex waveplates illuminated by Gaussian beams produce parasitic higher-order modes because the Gaussian profile mismatches the doughnut profile required for first-order vector beams, limiting the fidelity of the generated mode with respect to the target vector beam.
AI.method: The authors theoretically and experimentally use a spatial light modulator to generate a pseudovortex input, a doughnut-shaped mode without topological charge, and a geometric-phase-compensated triangular cavity for mode analysis. They compare vector-mode fidelity using Gaussian and pseudovortex inputs and investigate fidelity as a function of input beam waist.
AI.result: Vector mode fidelity reaches 0.921 ± 0.013 with pseudovortex input, compared with 0.815 ± 0.003 using Gaussian input. The theoretical upper bound is 8π/27 ≈ 0.931, in close agreement with experiment.
AI.conclusion: Pseudovortex illumination overcomes the fidelity limit imposed by Gaussian input and provides a reliable method for generating high-fidelity first-order vector modes such as radially and azimuthally polarized beams.

title: Inter-Nanoparticle Repulsion Effect on Self-Organization in Polymer Nanocomposites: A Langevin Dynamics Simulation Study
summary: Demixing through liquid-liquid phase separation is relevant to nanoparticle (NP) aggregation in polymer nanocomposites (PNCs), biomolecular compartmentalization, and liquids embedded in elastic networks. Mixing-demixing phase behavior depends on factors, such as particle size distribution, system dimen-sionality, intermolecular interactions, and relative concentrations. Here, using Langevin Dynamics simu-lations, we systematically investigate the effect of inter-nanoparticle repulsion on the self-assembly of PNCs under extreme confinement. A nanoparticle assembly, in the form of a compact droplet, is immersed in a polymer matrix of semiflexible, rod-like chains. By varying the nanoparticle-nanoparticle repulsion strength, while fixing all other interactions, we identify four distinct regimes with respect to the self-assembled NP morphologies: droplet, slab, crystalline droplet, and dispersed. Cluster-based analysis reveals a progressive loss of nanoparticle droplet integrity, leading to fragmentation within the dispersed regime. Local order of the nanoparticle assembly and global order of polymer chains are gauged through refined descriptors, quantifying the degrees of crystallinity and of nematic order, respectively. Interest-ingly, the slab regime exhibits negligible nanoparticle crystallization yet demonstrates the strongest polymer nematic ordering. In contrast, the crystalline droplet displays extensive triangular close-packed crystallites accompanied by a significant reduction in polymer nematic order, owing to its rhomboid shape. In the dispersed regime, nanoparticle fragmentation facilitates efficient mixing and local smectic-like ordering of the polymer chains. These findings demonstrate that fine-tuning inter-NP repulsions can control self-organization and the resulting morphologies, providing insights into PNCs with tailored functionality.

AI.motivation: Demixing via liquid-liquid phase separation is relevant to nanoparticle aggregation in polymer nanocomposites, biomolecular compartmentalization, and liquids in elastic networks. Because mixing-demixing behavior depends on particle size distribution, dimensionality, interactions, and concentrations, the paper systematically examines how inter-nanoparticle repulsion affects self-assembly under extreme confinement.
AI.method: The authors use Langevin dynamics simulations of a compact nanoparticle droplet immersed in a polymer matrix of semiflexible, rod-like chains under extreme confinement. They vary the nanoparticle-nanoparticle repulsion strength while fixing all other interactions, and use cluster-based analysis plus refined descriptors to quantify local nanoparticle crystallinity and global polymer nematic order.

Increasing repulsion progressively reduces droplet integrity and causes fragmentation in the dispersed regime. The slab regime shows negligible nanoparticle crystallization but the strongest polymer nematic ordering; the crystalline droplet contains extensive triangular close-packed crystallites and significantly reduced polymer nematic order due to its rhomboid shape; the dispersed regime enables efficient mixing and local smectic-like polymer ordering.

title: Access to the quasi-geostrophic model from within the BK19 compressible flow solver
summary: We extend BK19 the semi-implicit finite-volume solver, to provide access to the quasi-geostrophic (QG) regime within the same compressible framework that already admits soundproof and hydrostatic limits. In order to achieve this goal, we incorporate the asymptotic framework from the continuous theory into the numerical scheme. Adopting the usual asymptotic setting for the quasi-geostrophic regime and using it directly in the numerical model, we perform a scale analysis of the compressible Euler equations in the synoptic length and time scales in the limit of small Rossby number. In this limit, the discrete implicit step recovers geostrophic balance, together with the pseudo-incompressible divergence constraint. We construct a staggered-grid curl operator consistent with the discrete derivatives and use it to define the vorticity in the numerical framework. An asymptotic analysis of the fully discrete scheme then yields a Poisson-type equation for the leading-order Exner-pressure perturbation that coincides with the QG pressure Poisson equation in the continuous theory. As a result of this analysis, we introduce two additional blending switches that (i) convert the elliptic pressure problem from the full Helmholtz to its QG Poisson-type equation and (ii) control whether the horizontal momenta are updated prognostically or diagnosed from geostrophic balance. In combination with the existing soundproof and hydrostatic switches, the resulting algorithm can be operated in fully compressible, pseudo-incompressible, hydrostatic, and QG modes without changing the underlying discretization. The functionality of the numerical scheme in the QG regime is then tested by two idealized vortex test cases to show how stable the vortices remain in the QG run and that, as the Rossby number is reduced, the full compressible scheme converges to slow, balanced QG dynamics.

AI.tldr: The BK19 semi-implicit finite-volume compressible solver is extended to access the quasi-geostrophic regime through asymptotic analysis and new blending switches, allowing compressible, pseudo-incompressible, hydrostatic, and QG modes within one discretization. Idealized vortex tests show stable QG vortices and convergence to balanced QG dynamics as the Rossby number decreases.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to extend the BK19 semi-implicit finite-volume solver so that the quasi-geostrophic regime is accessible within the same compressible framework that already admits soundproof and hydrostatic limits, without changing the underlying discretization.
AI.method: The authors incorporate the continuous asymptotic framework for quasi-geostrophic flow into the numerical scheme. They perform a scale analysis of the compressible Euler equations at synoptic length and time scales in the small-Rossby-number limit, show that the discrete implicit step recovers geostrophic balance with the pseudo-incompressible divergence constraint, construct a staggered-grid curl operator consistent with the discrete derivatives to define vorticity, and asymptotically analyze the fully discrete scheme to obtain a Poisson-type equation for the leading-order Exner-pressure perturbation matching the continuous QG pressure Poisson equation. Two additional blending switches are introduced: one converts the elliptic pressure problem from the full Helmholtz to the QG Poisson-type equation, and the other controls whether horizontal momenta are updated prognostically or diagnosed from geostrophic balance.

Two idealized vortex test cases show that vortices remain stable in the QG run and that, as the Rossby number is reduced, the full compressible scheme converges to slow, balanced QG dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The BK19 solver can provide access to quasi-geostrophic dynamics within a single compressible finite-volume framework, with the QG limit realized through asymptotic-consistent discrete equations and blending switches; idealized vortex tests support the stability and convergence of the QG regime.

title: UV and deep-UV ultrafast harmonic generation enhanced by resonant gold nano-pillar metasurface
summary: We report experimental observations and full-vector numerical simulations of second and third-harmonic generation from a two-dimensional periodic gold nano-pillar metasurface, for efficient ultrafast light conversion from near-infrared to the UV and deep-UV spectral ranges. The metasurface is designed to support an angle-tunable plasmonic resonance in the near-infrared spectral range, with its resonance wavelength shifting as a function of the pump angle of incidence. Under resonant conditions, strong electromagnetic-field confinement near the nano-pillar corners enhances the nonlinear light-matter interactions. Compared with a flat gold mirror, the nanostructured metal exhibits enhanced nonlinear frequency conversion, with conversion efficiencies of second and third-harmonic generation increased by two and three orders of magnitude, respectively. Full-wave theoretical modeling of linear and nonlinear light-matter interaction in nanoscale structures validates the experimental results. We demonstrate that periodically arranged square gold pillars can be engineered to achieve enhanced second and third-harmonic generation at wavelengths that can be tailored through the structural design, without requiring complex geometries or hybrid structures that pose fabrication challenges. The close agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements further advances our understanding of surface-mediated nonlinear optical processes in metals and highlights the potential of metallic nanostructures as ultrafast light sources in the UV and deep-UV.

AI.tldr: A periodically arranged gold nano-pillar metasurface with an angle-tunable near-infrared plasmonic resonance enhances second- and third-harmonic generation for ultrafast near-infrared-to-UV and deep-UV light conversion; experiments and full-vector simulations show conversion efficiencies increased by two and three orders of magnitude, respectively, relative to a flat gold mirror.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to achieve efficient ultrafast light conversion from the near-infrared to the UV and deep-UV spectral ranges using a simple metallic nanostructure that avoids complex geometries or hybrid structures with fabrication challenges.
AI.method: The authors performed experimental observations and full-vector numerical simulations of second- and third-harmonic generation from a two-dimensional periodic gold nano-pillar metasurface. The metasurface supports an angle-tunable plasmonic resonance in the near-infrared, and resonant field confinement near the nano-pillar corners enhances nonlinear light-matter interactions. Performance was compared with a flat gold mirror, and full-wave theoretical modeling of linear and nonlinear interactions validated the measurements.
