Replacing detect-and-discard with error correction would increase the finite-key rate by a factor of 4.1–6.6 and yield a positive finite-key rate on the 142.9 km link where the implemented scheme yields none.
AI.conclusion: A deployed four-city entanglement-based QKD network with real-time key delivery and passive wavelength routing is demonstrated. Finite-key benchmarking exposes limitations of the implemented heuristic privacy amplification and indicates that error correction can substantially improve finite-key rates and extend positive-rate operation to longer links.

title: Implementation of a 1D Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD under finite-size parameter estimation
summary: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) is a promising technology for quantum-secure communications, offering high secret-key rates and straightforward integration with coherent optical communication systems. Conventional Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD encodes information in both optical-field quadratures, increasing requirements for state preparation, modulation, and calibration, while potentially introducing additional preparation imperfections. Unidimensional (1D) Gaussian modulation offers a simpler alternative by encoding information in only one quadrature, while the conjugate quadrature constrains the protocol's security. However, an integrated experimental 1D implementation combining independent-laser coherent reception with practical reconciliation, finite-size parameter estimation, and privacy amplification remains challenging. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a 1D Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD system over 12~km of standard single-mode fiber using a local local oscillator (LLO) architecture with independent lasers and an integrated offline classical post-processing chain. The implementation includes coherent detection, digital signal processing, information reconciliation, parameter estimation, physicality-constrained security analysis, and privacy amplification. The 1D system achieves a privacy-amplified rate of $1.421$~Mbit/s under the asymptotic security treatment and $0.364$~Mbit/s under the finite-size scenario. These results establish an experimental baseline for the performance--complexity trade-off associated with unidimensional Gaussian modulation and provide an experimental basis for developing lower-complexity CV-QKD transmitters.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates a unidimensional Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable quantum key distribution system over 12 km of standard single-mode fiber using a local local oscillator architecture with independent lasers and an integrated offline classical post-processing chain. It reports privacy-amplified rates of 1.421 Mbit/s under asymptotic security and 0.364 Mbit/s under finite-size security.
AI.motivation: Conventional Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD encodes information in both optical-field quadratures, which increases state-preparation, modulation, and calibration requirements and may introduce additional preparation imperfections. Unidimensional Gaussian modulation offers a simpler alternative by encoding information in only one quadrature, but an integrated experimental 1D implementation combining independent-laser coherent reception with practical reconciliation, finite-size parameter estimation, and privacy amplification remains challenging.
AI.method: The authors implement a 1D Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD system over 12 km of standard single-mode fiber using a local local oscillator architecture with independent lasers. The implementation includes coherent detection, digital signal processing, information reconciliation, parameter estimation, physicality-constrained security analysis, and privacy amplification within an integrated offline classical post-processing chain. Performance is evaluated under asymptotic and finite-size security treatments.
AI.result: The 1D system achieves a privacy-amplified rate of 1.421 Mbit/s under the asymptotic security treatment and 0.364 Mbit/s under the finite-size scenario over 12 km of standard single-mode fiber.
AI.conclusion: The results establish an experimental baseline for the performance-complexity trade-off of unidimensional Gaussian modulation and provide an experimental basis for developing lower-complexity CV-QKD transmitters.

title: Reflection Zeros Set the Scattering Invariant of Finite Majorana Wires
summary: Majorana modes, zero-energy excitations of superconducting wires that are their own antiparticles, could store quantum information protected from local noise. In transport experiments, however, ordinary bound states mimic their signature, a conductance peak at zero voltage, and whether Majorana modes have been observed remains debated. A sign, $Q$, of the electron reflection at zero energy marks the topological phase of a long wire, but what $Q$ certifies in a finite device has been unclear. Here we show for the first time that $Q$ counts reflectionless states, waves that enter through one contact and leave entirely through the other: $Q=-1$ when an odd number of them lie in the lower half of the complex energy plane. In a finite wire this means that the two Majorana modes are split by less than their coupling to the contacts. With equal contacts, every sign change of $Q$, including the bulk topological transition, is an exceptional point at which two such states merge and transmission is maximally flat. At zero temperature, $Q=-1$ exactly when the zero-bias conductance measured at a contact exceeds $e^2/h$. These results show what transport can certify about a Majorana device and how to read the invariant from conductance.

AI.tldr: The paper clarifies what the zero-energy electron-reflection sign Q certifies in finite Majorana wires by relating it to reflectionless scattering states, exceptional points, and zero-bias conductance.
AI.motivation: Majorana modes could store quantum information protected from local noise, but ordinary bound states can mimic their zero-voltage conductance peak, so it has been unclear what the reflection sign Q certifies in a finite device and what transport can establish about a Majorana device.
AI.method: The authors analyze the sign Q of zero-energy electron reflection in finite Majorana wires in terms of reflectionless states and their locations in the complex energy plane, including equal-contact and zero-temperature conductance conditions.
AI.result: Q counts reflectionless states: Q=-1 when an odd number lie in the lower half of the complex energy plane. In a finite wire this means the two Majorana modes are split by less than their coupling to the contacts. With equal contacts, every sign change of Q, including the bulk topological transition, is an exceptional point where two such states merge and transmission is maximally flat. At zero temperature, Q=-1 exactly when the zero-bias conductance at a contact exceeds e^2/h.
AI.conclusion: The results show what transport can certify about a Majorana device and how to read the scattering invariant from conductance.

title: Lorentz Boosts and Governing Equations of the Quantum Geometric Tensor in 4D Energy-Momentum Space
summary: In solids, the quantum geometric tensor (QGT), $Q_{μν}=g_{μν}-\frac{i}{2} Ω_{μν}$, combines the quantum metric and Berry curvature. Its imaginary part governs anomalous velocity and quantized Hall transport, while its real part determines the quantum weight and geometric contributions to flat-band superfluid stiffness and dielectric response. Here, we extend the QGT to four-dimensional (4D) energy-momentum space ($ω/c,k$), treating frequency and momentum as independent coordinates. Invariance of the real-spacetime plane-wave phase fixes their Lorentz transformation in energy-momentum space. Lorentz boosts of static Dirac and Weyl systems then generate frequency metrics, quadrupolar frequency-momentum shear metrics, and electric-like Berry-Maxwell fields. We identify five Lorentz-invariant contractions and derive the governing field equations and flow conservation laws for both the quantum metric and Berry curvature from static Weyl geometry and Lorentz covariance. We further connect Gaussian spectral amplitudes of the QGT to localized Gaussian events in 4D spacetime. Finally, we discuss experimental realizations in spacetime crystals or time-varying media and clarify how this unified quantum geometry of a gravitational-like metric and electromagnetic-like gauge fields connects geometric self-consistency with physical event dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the quantum geometric tensor from its usual solid-state form to a four-dimensional energy-momentum space, derives Lorentz-covariant field equations and conservation laws for its quantum-metric and Berry-curvature parts, and links Gaussian spectral amplitudes to localized spacetime events, with proposed realizations in spacetime crystals or time-varying media.
AI.motivation: The quantum geometric tensor combines the quantum metric and Berry curvature: its imaginary part governs anomalous velocity and quantized Hall transport, while its real part determines the quantum weight and geometric contributions to flat-band superfluid stiffness and dielectric response. The authors aim to generalize this framework to 4D energy-momentum space with frequency and momentum treated as independent coordinates.
AI.method: The authors treat frequency and momentum as independent coordinates in 4D energy-momentum space. They use invariance of the real-spacetime plane-wave phase to fix the Lorentz transformation of these coordinates, apply Lorentz boosts to static Dirac and Weyl systems, identify five Lorentz-invariant contractions, and derive governing field equations and flow conservation laws for the quantum metric and Berry curvature from static Weyl geometry and Lorentz covariance. They also connect Gaussian spectral amplitudes of the quantum geometric tensor to localized Gaussian events in 4D spacetime.
AI.result: Lorentz boosts of static Dirac and Weyl systems generate frequency metrics, quadrupolar frequency-momentum shear metrics, and electric-like Berry-Maxwell fields. The paper identifies five Lorentz-invariant contractions and derives governing field equations and flow conservation laws for both the quantum metric and Berry curvature. It further establishes a connection between Gaussian spectral amplitudes of the quantum geometric tensor and localized Gaussian events in 4D spacetime. Experimental realizations are discussed for spacetime crystals or time-varying media; no experimental data are reported.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified quantum geometry combining a gravitational-like metric with electromagnetic-like gauge fields and clarifies how geometric self-consistency connects with physical event dynamics. It proposes spacetime crystals and time-varying media as possible experimental platforms.

title: Hong$-$Ou$-$Mandel-like interference between two independent narrowband thermal states
summary: Narrowband photonic sources are promising candidates in quantum networks for a direct interface with atomic quantum memories. However, building a large-scale quantum network requires many indistinguishable sources, and matching the frequencies of independent narrowband sources is generally challenging. Here, we propose a method to measure the frequency difference between two narrowband light sources in the single-photon power regime by studying Hong$-$Ou$-$Mandel-like (HOM) interference between thermal states. Our results show that the absolute value of the frequency difference can be extracted from the temporal coincidence counts, and these results agree well with our theoretical model. We also demonstrate that the beat signal of the HOM-like interference between two thermal states has a similar oscillation profile to the HOM interference between two heralded single-photon sources, confirming that this method can be used to find the zero detuning of two heralded single-photon sources.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and experimentally supports a method to measure the absolute frequency difference between two independent narrowband thermal light sources in the single-photon power regime using Hong–Ou–Mandel-like interference, with potential application to zero-detuning alignment of heralded single-photon sources.
AI.motivation: Large-scale quantum networks require many indistinguishable narrowband photonic sources that can interface with atomic quantum memories, but matching the frequencies of independent narrowband sources is generally challenging.
AI.method: The authors study Hong–Ou–Mandel-like interference between two independent narrowband thermal states in the single-photon power regime and extract the absolute frequency difference from temporal coincidence counts; they compare the results with a theoretical model and examine the beat signal relative to HOM interference between two heralded single-photon sources.
AI.result: The absolute value of the frequency difference can be extracted from temporal coincidence counts, and the results agree well with the theoretical model. The beat signal of the thermal-state HOM-like interference shows a similar oscillation profile to HOM interference between two heralded single-photon sources.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method can measure the frequency difference between independent narrowband thermal sources in the single-photon power regime and can be used to find the zero detuning of two heralded single-photon sources, supporting frequency matching for quantum-network applications.

title: Non-Convex Optimization via Quantum Tunneling Search on a Photonic Chip
summary: Non-convex optimization plays an important role in modern machine learning since plenty of real-world problems have objective functions or constraints with non-convex properties. The non-convex nature of landscapes gives rise to numerous local minima and saddle points, dramatically hindering the ability of gradient descent-based methods to explore the landscape and obtain global optima. Here we present quantum tunneling search (QTS), an algorithm based on quantum tunneling walk and local annealing, which effectively explores the non-convex landscape by leveraging the quantum tunneling effect. In experiments, we map an objective function to the potential term of the waveguide Hamiltonian by controlling the refractive index with the femtosecond direct laser writing technique. With a proper input state, the average probability distributions on 10-micrometer-spaced 29 x 1 and 21 x 9 waveguide arrays highlight the local minima of various 1D and 2D non-convex landscapes, respectively. By further introducing the varying Hamiltonian approach, more efficient search and even the identification of the global minimum are achieved. Our work experimentally verifies that QTS is a successful and efficient non-convex optimization solver, demonstrating quantum speedups over classical stochastic gradient descent (SGD), which serves as a practical application of near-term analog quantum simulators in the field of machine learning.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates quantum tunneling search (QTS), a quantum-tunneling-walk plus local-annealing algorithm, on photonic waveguide arrays fabricated by femtosecond direct laser writing, showing efficient exploration of 1D and 2D non-convex landscapes and quantum speedups over classical stochastic gradient descent.
AI.motivation: Non-convex optimization is central to machine learning, but local minima and saddle points impede gradient descent-based methods from exploring landscapes and finding global optima.
AI.method: The authors propose QTS, combining a quantum tunneling walk with local annealing. They map an objective function to the potential term of a waveguide Hamiltonian by controlling the refractive index via femtosecond direct laser writing, use suitable input states in 10-micrometer-spaced 29 x 1 and 21 x 9 waveguide arrays, and introduce a varying Hamiltonian approach.
AI.result: Average probability distributions highlight local minima of various 1D and 2D non-convex landscapes. The varying Hamiltonian approach enables more efficient search and identification of the global minimum. The work experimentally verifies QTS as an efficient non-convex optimizer and reports quantum speedups over classical stochastic gradient descent; quantitative speedup values are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: QTS is a successful and efficient non-convex optimization solver, demonstrating a practical application of near-term analog quantum simulators in machine learning.

title: Reply to the Comment by Hradil and Řeháček
summary: Hradil and Řeháček argue that the quantum metrological advantage demonstrated in our squeezed-vacuum phase-sensing experiment disappears, when measurement repetitions and total photon resources are properly accounted for. We show that this conclusion is mathematically unfounded and that neither resource accounting nor finite-sample statistical considerations invalidate the demonstrated quantum-enhanced local phase sensitivity.

AI.tldr: The authors rebut a comment claiming that their squeezed-vacuum phase-sensing advantage vanishes under proper accounting of measurement repetitions and total photon resources, arguing that the critique is mathematically unfounded and that the quantum-enhanced local phase sensitivity remains valid.

title: Non-Bloch Topology of Frustrated Non-Hermitian Flat Bands
summary: Frustrated lattices with exactly flat bands and compact localized states provide an ideal setting to uncover the topology of flat bands, leading to intriguing physics in two dimensions. To characterize the correspondence, an invariant is proposed based on biorthogonal polarization of the zero-energy corner mode. Breaking exact flatness, we further realize nearly flat non-Bloch Chern bands.

title: Exact transformation-optics representation of the Ellis wormhole and limits of finite-device scattering emulation

summary: We derive a global isotropic representation of the ultrastatic Ellis wormhole and establish which features of its electromagnetic response can, and cannot, be reproduced by a finite device. An orientation-preserving coordinate map sends the signed proper-radial line to a punctured Euclidean chart with refractive index $n(ρ)=1+a^2/(4ρ^2)$. Through the Plebański correspondence, this gives the exact impedance-matched continuum medium $\varepsilon_r=μ_r=n(ρ)\,\mathbb{1}$ and its full vector-Maxwell operator. For the ideal two-ended geometry, we derive the electromagnetic radial operator, establish its spectral properties, and express its scattering amplitudes through Jost solutions and Wronskians. Nonzero transmission into the second asymptotic end implies $|R_{\rm id}|<1$ at every real frequency, whereas a regular, lossless finite one-port has unit-modulus reflection. The transmission cross section tends to $πa^2$, while the ideal profile's total scattering cross section has a logarithmic forward divergence. We also construct a smooth finite-shell target and derive an exact finite-band constitutive-error formula for a calibrated passive Lorentz model. The constitutive benchmark is kept distinct from scattering equivalence throughout.

title: Towards Distributed Quantum Computing: Quantum Gate Teleportation via Satellite-Distributed Entanglement under Atmospheric Depolarization
summary: We investigate quantum gate teleportation as a primitive for satellite-enabled distributed quantum computing. In the considered architecture, a satellite distributes entangled photon pairs to two optical ground stations, which transfer the shared quantum resource to remote quantum processing units. This entanglement is then used to implement a nonlocal controlled-NOT gate between two circuit qubits located in different processors. We formulate the minimal four-qubit protocol, consisting of two network qubits that provide the entangled resource and two circuit qubits on which the distributed gate is performed. Atmospheric propagation effects in the gravitational field are modeled through an effective two-qubit depolarizing channel whose parameters depend on atmospheric and optical quantities, including the Fried parameter and receiver aperture. The performance of the protocol is quantified by the fidelity between the ideal CNOT output state and the state produced by noisy quantum gate teleportation. Our results show that the fidelity is governed by the quality of the distributed entanglement and depends jointly on atmospheric coherence, aperture size, and effective depolarization strength. These findings connect physical-layer modeling of satellite optical channels with gate-level performance in distributed quantum computing.
